Submission received: 25 November 2022 / Revised: 15 December 2022 / Accepted: 18 December 2022 / Published: 21 December 2022 Abstract Studying waterlogged archaeological wood moisture characteristics can provide strong support for the safe dehydration and preservation of waterlogged wooden artifacts. Herein, six waterlogged archaeological wood samples with moisture contents of 154%–968% chosen from two ancient Chinese shipwrecks, Nanhai No. 1 and Changjiangkou No. 2, and six non-degraded modern wood samples of the relevant corresponding species were selected to study the moisture characteristics by low-temperature nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and the dynamic sorption of water vapor (DVS). It was found that the six waterlogged archaeological wood samples exhibited three deterioration states: slightly, moderately, and seriously deteriorated. Wood deterioration caused significantly increased fiber saturation point (FSP) values for waterlogged archaeological wood. This is mainly owing to changes in the pore size distribution of cell walls. Moreover, NMR is more accurate than DVS in obtaining FSP for severely degraded samples. Additionally, moisture content was positively associated with wood deterioration. Maximum water content (MWC), free water content, and bound water content exhibited an exponential relationship with the basic density (BD). The contribution of bound water in waterlogged archaeological wood was less than that of modern wood and decreased with deterioration. 1. Introduction Wood is one of the most common biomass materials and is widely used in handicrafts, furniture, building, and ship manufacturing [1,2,3,4]. Therefore, a lot of wooden artifacts have been excavated around the world; some of them have been excavated from underwater (i.e., rivers, lakes, and seas). Compared with wood products in other environments, wood products unearthed underwater are saturated with water (or seawater). Some wood products have even been submerged in water for centuries, e.g., the shipwrecks of the Roman ship San Rossore, the warship Vasa in Stockholm, Sweden, the Mary Rose in Portsmouth, UK, the Bremen Cog in Germany, and the Nanhai No. 1 in China [5,6,7,8,9]. These recovered artifacts reflect the level of scientific and technological productivity under their specific historical periods and are thus precious resources. The most common form of microbial attack in waterlogged environments is erosion bacteria [10,11]. Erosion bacteria enter the cell lumen through wood rays and pits, starting from the S3 layer to digest cellulose and hemicellulose in the cell wall, then attacking the S2 layer. In the late stage of decay, lignin residues are left in the S2 layer, while the lignin-rich composite intermediate layer remains intact [12]. Waterlogged wood retains its original appearance after being attacked by bacteria, but has significantly reduced physical and mechanical properties and even becomes very soft and easily deformed or collapses when dry [13]. Since drying waterlogged archaeological woodwork is a necessary condition for museumization [14], this poses a significant challenge for protecting waterlogged archaeological wood from dehydration. The effective and safe removal of moisture is the key and prerequisite for wooden cultural relics to be separated from degradation environments, for cultural information extraction, and storage environment preservation. The conservation treatment of waterlogged archaeological wood is not complete until it has been dried to remove any residual moisture, a prerequisite for the collection [15]. The moisture characteristics of waterlogged archaeological wood are fundamental to the development of dehydration preservation technologies. Degradation of the waterlogged archaeological wood results in a large number of pores in the secondary wall, reducing the strength of the cell wall [12,16]. The resulting pores cause more water to enter the wood [5,10,17]. Until now, waterlogged archaeological wood has been studied quite extensively and comprehensively and has mainly focused on deterioration state assessment [18,19,20], microbial reactions [21,22,23], sediment reactions [24,25,26], chemical degradation [27,28,29], physical degradation [18,30], sorption behaviors [31,32], and the synthesis and characterization of fixatives [33,34,35,36,37]. However, little information has been reported on the moisture characteristics of waterlogged archaeological wood. However, understanding the moisture characteristics of waterlogged archaeological wood is essential for its conservation. During the post excavation phase of storage and restoration, the presence of oxygen makes waterlogged archaeological wood extremely vulnerable to biodegradation hazards [38]. Therefore, waterlogged archaeological wood must be protected as soon as it is unearthed. However, reinforcement and proper drying procedures must be implemented to prevent irreparable collapse and damage [39]. fetched_contents.text: Complementary Raman and FTIR spectroscopic insights into lignin removal from poplar using deep eutectic solvents Highlights * • Systematically compared SCARS, CARS, MC-UVE, and iMWPLS for lignin prediction. * • Revealed the complementary variable distributions between Raman and infrared spectra. * • Established optimal strategies: iMWPLS for single-spectrum and MC-UVE for fused spectra. * • Linked spectral monitoring with reduced chemical usage and enhanced sustainability. Abstract Accurate and rapid quantitative determination of lignin is crucial for evaluating biomass processing and value-added applications. This study systematically investigated the applicability of variable selection methods—SCARS, CARS, MC-UVE, iMWPLS for predicting lignin content. Results indicate that full-spectrum Raman modeling exhibits limited predictive accuracy (Rp2=0.6221, RMSEP=1.8779). The fused spectra exhibited stronger complementary information effects. Under full-spectrum modeling, the Rp2 value of the fused spectrum reached 0.7585—22.0% higher than Raman and 8.8% higher than ATR-FTIR—while RMSEP was 1.2923, significantly lower than Raman (31.2% reduction) and marginally better than ATR-FTIR. Under fusion conditions, MC-UVE achieved optimal results (Rp2=0.8657, RMSEP=1.0561), representing a 14.1% improvement and 18.3% reduction compared to the full spectrum, while also outperforming the optimal models from single spectra. This study revealed the differences and complementarity in feature variable distributions between Raman and infrared spectroscopy, emphasizing the critical role of variable selection methods in enhancing modeling accuracy. It provides a novel technical pathway for rapid quantitative detection of lignin. The application of spectral techniques significantly reduces reliance on wet chemical analysis, enabling real-time, non-destructive monitoring of the lignin removal process. This methodological advancement lays the groundwork for subsequent life cycle assessments—where the adoption of spectral monitoring is expected to decrease analytical energy consumption and chemical usage. Keywords Lignin content ; Infrared spectrum ; Quantitative analysis ; Life cycle assessment Introduction Lignocellulosic biomass represents the most abundant renewable organic carbon source on Earth. Its efficient development and utilization are crucial for reducing dependence on fossil resources and advancing the establishment of sustainable energy and material systems [1], [2]. Lignocellulose primarily consists of three major components: cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Lignin, a complex aromatic polymer formed by the random polymerization of phenylpropane units, accounts for 15–30 % of biomass dry weight [3]. Lignin confers mechanical strength and hydrophobicity to plant cell walls but is often regarded as a “barrier component” that is difficult to degrade and utilize during biomass conversion [4], [5]. fetched_contents.text: A review of analytical methods for assessing preservation in waterlogged archaeological wood and their application in practice Introduction and background Assessing the current state of preservation of waterlogged archaeological wood provides vital information on decay trajectories, archaeological significance (the state of preservation is likely to influence the level of detail that can be retrieved from an object), and the potential consequences of changing conditions [1, 2]. Appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which any further deterioration can be tracked, for example: when a site is being monitored [3, 4], when comparing material from different sites or phases of investigation [5, 6], or when gathering experimental data on decay mechanisms [7,8,9]. Analysis is also important post-excavation; detecting decay over periods of storage or display can help identify when conditions are not conducive to the continued survival of an object [10, 11]. Analysis during or after conservation can be a critical part of establishing when a conservation treatment has worked, or indeed is having a negative effect [12, 13]. Understanding the structure of wood, the potential decay mechanisms acting upon it, and appropriate techniques that can be used to assess and track these mechanisms is therefore important for archaeologists, conservators, and heritage management professionals. The structure and decay of waterlogged archaeological wood Fresh wood is made up of a system of cells composed of three major biopolymers, closely linked and arranged in fibrils (Fig. 1). The first of these, lignin, composes roughly 25–35% by mass, whilst cellulose and hemi-celluloses (two types of polysaccharide) together make up roughly 65–75%. A variety of ‘extractives’ (non-structural components such as pectins, tannins, resins, and oils) contribute up to 10% by mass. An in-depth description of the anatomical structure of wood is outside the scope of this review but can be found in e.g. [14,15,16]. Archaeological wood is subjected to a variety of both chemical and biological decay processes during its deposition and burial, resulting in a material with a very different chemical composition and structure to fresh wood [14, 17]. Under the anoxic conditions provided by waterlogged environments, decay processes are significantly slowed and primarily driven by anaerobic biological agents [15, 18, 19]. These agents preferentially attack polysaccharides via enzymatic degradation, with hemi-celluloses being particularly vulnerable [15, 20]. Some studies demonstrate that chemical deterioration of cellulose also occurs in waterlogged environments, particularly under extreme conditions such as low pH [6, 10]. Lignin is generally considered to be much more resistant to biological decay, largely due to its highly stable structure: a large 3 dimensional network of cross-linked polyphenol sub units (Fig. 1; [20]. The preferential decay of celluloses means that waterlogged archaeological wood is often characterised by a high lignin content, with celluloses completely depleted in some cases [21, 22]. In waterlogged environments, the cellulose-depleted cell walls become instead filled with water, allowing the structure of the wood to be maintained [20]. However, this lignin-rich skeleton is a very fragile material that is highly susceptible to mechanical damage and can collapse or warp very easily when dried [12, 23]. Although comparatively stable, decay of lignin does also occur. In particular, certain anaerobic fungi digest lignin via enzymatic oxidation [15, 21]. This results in modification of the sub-units, for example an increased concentration of the more resistant guaiacyl-type lignin compared to syringyl-type is often observed in decayed wood [16, 17]. Exchange with the burial environment can influence the chemical composition of waterlogged archaeological wood. Many ‘extractives’ are water soluble, and therefore present in drastically lower concentrations or completely absent [14, 17]. The highly porous nature of wood means that minerals from the burial environment (such as iron sulfides, phosphates and calcium) may become incorporated into the cell walls over time, resulting in a higher inorganic, or ‘ash’ content [17, 24]. A particularly problematic process is the build-up of sulfur salts in wood from marine environments, as these can oxidise when exposed to air and form sulfuric acid, leading to subsequent hydrolysis of cellulose [25, 26]. The presence of iron (e.g. from nails) alongside sulfur in particular can lead to the formation of a wide range of salts within the cellular structure, which leads to extensive mechanical damage if they occupy more volume than the precursor molecules [26, 27]. The identification of inorganic components can be critical for predicting the success of conservation treatments and the possible effects of long-term storage. Challenges in the analysis of waterlogged archaeological wood Analysis of waterlogged archaeological wood aims to evaluate these chemical and physical changes in order to determine its current state of preservation. This knowledge is vital in informing conservation or management of these objects: an adequate assessment supplies a baseline against which future change can be measured, and provides an indication of whether further changes might be expected as a result of the proposed strategy [1, 12]. However, the complexity of waterlogged archaeological wood, particularly its highly heterogeneous nature, presents significant analytical challenges. As deterioration tends to occur first at the surface and progress inwards there is often a gradient of decay, with the inner heartwood much better preserved than the outer sapwood [12, 15]. Different species of erosion microorganisms will also result in different patterns of decay [15]. Branch report: Raman spectroscopy strengths and weaknesses for waterlogged wood

Raman spectroscopy is well suited to identifying the main organic components in waterlogged wood, especially lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose. The evidence says Raman spectra of wood tissues “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], and that Raman spectroscopy has been used to analyze archaeological wood specimens, including identification of organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin [N1-R4]. That makes Raman useful for recognizing the major biopolymer classes and some extractive-like compounds in wood.

A key strength is non-destructive sampling. Raman is described as non-invasive and as offering advantages such as high speed, robust identification, low cost, and portability [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This is especially valuable for fragile waterlogged wood, where destructive sampling is undesirable or impractical. The review also notes that portable Raman can enable in situ analysis without moving fragile remains [N1-R3]. This non-destructive and portable nature is a major practical advantage for archaeological wood, which is often fragile and difficult to transport.

Raman also has specific compound-detection strengths. The evidence explicitly states that Raman can identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin in archaeological specimens [N1-R4]. It also emphasizes that Raman is useful for characterizing lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose in wood tissues [N5-R1]. In this sense, Raman is strong for detecting molecular markers that are otherwise difficult to isolate without destructive pretreatment.

Water content and moisture have a major impact on Raman signal quality and interpretation. The context provided shows that waterlogged wood can have moisture contents as high as 154%–968% [N3-F4], and that deterioration increases fiber saturation point and pore size distribution [N3-F4]. While the evidence does not directly give a Raman-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that high water content and deterioration alter the physical and chemical state of wood, which can affect how light interacts with the sample. The review also states that Raman has been used in waterlogged archaeological wood conservation studies [N6-F1], suggesting that researchers have already addressed moisture-related challenges in this context. Still, the provided evidence does not provide a detailed Raman-specific moisture artifact profile, so this point remains contextually supported rather than fully quantified [N3-F4][N6-F1].

Sample preparation and handling issues are another limitation. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood analysis often requires specialized preparation, including drying, mounting, and handling that avoids damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. It also indicates that the wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis, which implies some handling effort [N4-R4]. The review notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is vulnerable to biodegradation hazards after excavation, so careful preservation and drying are necessary before analysis [N6-F1]. For Raman, the main handling issue is that the sample must be prepared without excessive drying or mechanical stress, which can distort the structure and reduce the reliability of the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4]. In other words, Raman is sensitive to preparation quality and sample integrity, which can be harder to control in waterlogged wood.

Overall, the branch picture is that Raman is strong for non-destructive, portable, and specific compound detection in waterlogged wood, especially lignin and cellulose, but it faces limitations from moisture-related signal complexity and the need for careful sample preparation and handling [N1-R1][N1-R3][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].
node_outputs.N10:
Branch report: FTIR strengths and weaknesses for waterlogged wood

FTIR is also well suited to identifying the main molecular components of waterlogged wood, particularly cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractives. The evidence explicitly says FTIR and pyrolysis have been used to characterize wood components, which mainly include cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, extracts, and ash [N2-R3]. It also states that FTIR is widely used in qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood because of its ability to provide information about functional groups [N2-R4]. In the waterlogged context, FTIR is practical for evaluating bacterial wood degradation and is used for assessing preservation in archaeological wood [N2-R1][N6-F1]. This makes FTIR especially useful for identifying the major biopolymers and any extractive-like or mineral components in waterlogged wood.

A key strength of FTIR is that it is often more readily available in common laboratory settings and is practical for routine analysis. The evidence notes that FTIR measurements are practical in evaluating bacterial degradation in softwood [N2-R1], and that FTIR is widely used because it provides functional-group information [N2-R4]. This suggests that FTIR is a common, accessible technique for wood analysis. Another strength is speed and practicality. The review emphasizes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which future deterioration can be tracked, and that FTIR is among the most commonly reported methods for waterlogged archaeological wood [N6-F1]. This makes FTIR a strong option when the goal is a quick assessment or when sample numbers are large.

Water content and moisture also affect FTIR signal quality and interpretation. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood can have very high moisture content, and that moisture content is positively associated with deterioration [N3-F4]. It also indicates that moisture can influence the physical and chemical state of wood, including pore size distribution and bound/free water fractions [N3-F4]. Although the evidence does not provide a detailed FTIR-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that moisture and deterioration can distort the sample’s structure and chemistry, which can in turn affect FTIR interpretation. The review also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This is a direct limitation for FTIR in waterlogged wood, because high moisture can create baseline shifts, broadening, or overlapping peaks that reduce specificity [N5-F3].

Sample preparation and handling issues are another limitation. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood analysis often requires drying, mounting, and handling that avoids damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. It also notes that wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis [N4-R4]. For FTIR, the main issue is that the sample must be prepared carefully, especially in the case of waterlogged wood, where drying or mounting can alter the structure and affect the signal. The evidence also indicates that waterlogged wood can be preserved for many years in the absence of air, but once exposed to air or drying, biodegradation hazards increase [N6-F1]. This means that FTIR preparation may need to balance preservation of the sample with the need to make it suitable for infrared analysis, which can be challenging [N4-R1][N4-R4].

Overall, FTIR is strong for routine, accessible, and functional-group-based analysis of waterlogged wood, especially cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extracts, but it faces limitations from moisture artifacts, matrix background effects, and the need for careful sample preparation [N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-F3][N4-R1][N4-R4].
node_outputs.N11:
Branch report: comparative interpretation and technical limits

The evidence suggests that neither Raman nor FTIR is universally superior for distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives in waterlogged wood, but they do differ in how well they can do so. For lignin, the evidence indicates that Raman is particularly strong because it can detect aromatic ring skeletal vibrations and is less susceptible to moisture interference [N5-F3]. It also says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods and that their feature-variable distributions differ [N5-R2]. For cellulose, the evidence is more general: Raman spectra “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], while FTIR is described as providing information about functional groups and being widely used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood [N2-R4]. However, the review also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This implies that FTIR can struggle with ambiguity, especially when the sample is highly heterogeneous or moist.

The major spectral overlap and ambiguity problems are real for both techniques. The evidence says that Raman and FTIR have differences and complementarity in feature-variable distributions, but also that most peak positions in complex samples cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-R2][N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where the material is chemically and physically heterogeneous, and where moisture can broaden peaks or create baseline artifacts [N3-F4][N5-F3]. The review further notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous, with deterioration often occurring first at the surface and progressing inward, and that different species of erosion microorganisms produce different decay patterns [N6-F1]. This heterogeneity makes interpretation difficult for both techniques, because the same spectrum may reflect different decay states or different regions of the same sample [N6-F1].

Which technique is better suited to waterlogged wood depends on the preservation condition. For severely waterlogged or highly moist samples, Raman may be better because it is less susceptible to moisture interference [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that FTIR is affected by moisture and matrix backgrounds [N5-F3], which makes it less reliable under extremely high moisture conditions. In contrast, FTIR may be more practical when the sample is relatively stable or when the laboratory has established handling routines for waterlogged wood, because it is widely used and accessible [N2-R4][N6-F1]. The review also notes that a multi-analytical approach is vital, because no single technique gives the best assessment [N6-F1]. This implies that for some preservation conditions, FTIR is still the better choice for routine assessment, while Raman is better when moisture or heterogeneity make FTIR less reliable [N2-R4][N5-F3][N6-F1].

Complementary use of Raman and FTIR can improve interpretation. The evidence directly states that the two techniques are complementary, with differences and complementarity in feature-variable distributions [N5-R2][N5-F3]. It also says that spectral monitoring can reduce reliance on wet chemical analysis and improve detection of lignin removal [N5-F3]. In the context of waterlogged wood, this means combining the two can help overcome ambiguity: Raman can provide more specific lignin and aromatic information, while FTIR can offer functional-group resolution and broader quantitative information [N5-R2][N5-F3]. ## Main advantages and limitations of Raman versus FTIR for analyzing waterlogged archaeological wood

This comparison should be read as a practical guide to choosing between two complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods for waterlogged archaeological wood. The evidence from the branch reports shows that neither technique is universally superior for every preservation condition, but they do differ in how well they identify molecular components, handle moisture, and support interpretation. Below is a structured comparison of their main advantages and limitations.

---

### 1) What each method is best suited to identify

**Raman spectroscopy** is especially strong for identifying the major organic components in waterlogged wood, especially **lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose**. The evidence states that Raman spectra “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], and that Raman has been used in archaeological wood analysis to identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin [N1-R4]. It is also useful for detecting aromatic ring vibrations, which is important for lignin [N5-F3].

**FTIR** is also well suited to identifying the main molecular components of waterlogged wood, particularly **cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractives**. The evidence says FTIR and pyrolysis have been used to characterize wood components including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, extracts, and ash [N2-R3], and that FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4]. FTIR is also practical for evaluating bacterial wood degradation [N2-R1].

So, for waterlogged wood:
- **Raman is especially good for lignin and aromatic structural features** [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is especially good for cellulose, hemicellulose, and functional-group-based analysis** [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- Both are useful for extractives and other non-structural components, though the evidence is more explicit for FTIR in this regard [N2-R3].

---

### 2) Main practical advantages

#### Raman advantages
- **Non-destructive sampling** is a major advantage. Raman is described as non-invasive and as offering advantages such as high speed, robust identification, low cost, and portability [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This is especially valuable for fragile waterlogged wood, where destructive sampling is undesirable [N1-R3].
- **Portable and in situ use** is also a practical strength. Portable Raman can enable in situ analysis without moving fragile remains [N1-R3].
- **Specific compound detection** is another strength. Raman can identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin in archaeological specimens [N1-R4], which can help distinguish extractive-like compounds and other organic markers [N1-R4].

#### FTIR advantages
- **Common laboratory availability** is a strong practical advantage. FTIR is described as practical in evaluating bacterial degradation in softwood and as widely used because it provides functional-group information [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Speed and routine use** are also important. The review notes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which future deterioration can be tracked, and that FTIR is among the most commonly reported methods for waterlogged archaeological wood [N6-F1]. This makes it a strong option for routine assessment or when sample numbers are large.
- **Functional-group resolution** is another benefit. FTIR is useful for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood because of its ability to provide information about functional groups [N2-R4].

So, if the priority is **portability, non-destructiveness, and specific compound detection**, Raman is often the better choice. If the priority is **common availability, speed, and routine functional-group analysis**, FTIR is often the better choice.

---

### 3) Main limitations

#### Raman limitations
- **Moisture and water content can affect signal quality and interpretation**. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood can have very high moisture content, and that moisture content is positively associated with deterioration [N3-F4]. While the evidence does not give a detailed Raman-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that moisture and deterioration alter the physical and chemical state of wood, which can affect how the sample is analyzed [N3-F4][N6-F1]. The review also states that Raman has been used in waterlogged archaeological wood conservation studies [N6-F1], indicating that researchers have already addressed moisture-related challenges, but the evidence does not specify what those exact solutions are [N6-F1].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are a major limitation. Waterlogged wood analysis often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling to avoid damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that the wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis, which implies some handling effort [N4-R4]. For Raman, this means the sample must be prepared carefully without excessive drying or mechanical stress, which can distort the structure and reduce the reliability of the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### FTIR limitations
- **Moisture and matrix background effects** are a major limitation. The evidence states that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where moisture can broaden peaks, create baseline shifts, or make interpretation more ambiguous [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are also important. Waterlogged wood often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis [N4-R4]. For FTIR, the main issue is that the sample must be prepared carefully, especially in the case of waterlogged wood, where drying or mounting can alter the structure and affect the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Interpretation complexity** is another limitation. The review notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous, with deterioration often occurring first at the surface and progressing inward, and that different species of erosion microorganisms produce different decay patterns [N6-F1]. This heterogeneity makes interpretation difficult, because the same spectrum may reflect different decay states or different regions of the same sample [N6-F1].

The evidence suggests that neither technique is universally superior for distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives, but they do differ in how well they can do so.

- **FTIR is better for functional-group resolution**. However, it also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This makes FTIR less reliable for unambiguous identification of individual components when the sample is highly heterogeneous or moist [N5-F3].

This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where the material is chemically and physically heterogeneous [N6-F1].

- If the goal is **specific lignin identification**, Raman may be more reliable [N5-F3].

---

### 5) Which technique is better suited to waterlogged wood under different preservation conditions

The evidence points to a conditional conclusion:

- **Highly heterogeneous or degraded samples may require both techniques**. The review emphasizes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration patterns can vary by microorganism and burial environment [N6-F1]. In such cases, the best approach is often a multi-analytical strategy, because no single technique gives the best assessment [N6-F1].

So, the best choice depends on:
- **Moisture level**: Raman may be better for highly waterlogged wood [N5-F3].
- **Sample heterogeneity**: both techniques face ambiguity, but a combined approach is often better [N6-F1].
- **Practical constraints**: FTIR is more commonly available and faster, while Raman is more portable and non-destructive [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R4].

---

### 6) How complementary use of Raman and FTIR can improve interpretation

The evidence explicitly supports complementary use. The evidence says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods and that their feature-variable distributions differ [N5-R2]. It also says that spectral monitoring can reduce reliance on wet chemical analysis and improve detection of lignin removal [N5-F3]. In the context of waterlogged wood, this means:
- **Raman can provide more specific lignin and aromatic information**, especially in moist conditions [N5-F3].
- **FTIR can provide broader functional-group resolution and quantitative information**, especially when the sample is relatively stable [N2-R4].
- Together, they can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3].

The review also emphasizes that a multi-analytical approach is vital for obtaining a clear picture of the present state of decay [N6-F1]. This is important because waterlogged wood is chemically and physically heterogeneous, and because different preservation conditions may affect one technique more than the other [N6-F1].

---

### 7) Bottom-line conclusion

For **waterlogged archaeological wood**, the main conclusion is:

- **Raman is better when**: the sample is fragile, moisture-sensitive, or the goal is non-destructive, portable, or specific compound detection, especially for lignin [N1-R1][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is better when**: the sample can be prepared and analyzed under routine conditions, and the goal is accessible, fast, functional-group-based, or routine preservation assessment [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Neither is clearly superior for all preservation conditions**. Both face limitations from moisture, heterogeneity, and matrix effects [N3-F4][N5-F3][N6-F1].
- **Complementary use is often the best practical choice**. Combining Raman and FTIR can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

In short: Raman is the more modern, non-destructive, and moisture-tolerant option for some contexts; FTIR is the more established, accessible, and functional-group-oriented option for others. For waterlogged archaeological wood, the best approach is often to use both where possible, because no single technique alone gives the complete picture [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

## Main advantages and limitations of Raman versus FTIR for analyzing waterlogged archaeological wood

This comparison should be read as a practical guide to choosing between two complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods for waterlogged archaeological wood. The evidence from the branch reports shows that neither technique is universally superior for every preservation condition, but they do differ in how well they identify molecular components, handle moisture, and support interpretation. Below is a structured comparison of their main advantages and limitations.

---

### 1) What each method is best suited to identify

**Raman spectroscopy** is especially strong for identifying the major organic components in waterlogged wood, especially **lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose**. The evidence states that Raman spectra “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], and that Raman has been used in archaeological wood analysis to identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin [N1-R4]. It is also useful for detecting aromatic ring vibrations, which is important for lignin [N5-F3].

**FTIR** is also well suited to identifying the main molecular components of waterlogged wood, particularly **cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractives**. The evidence says FTIR and pyrolysis have been used to characterize wood components including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, extracts, and ash [N2-R3], and that FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4]. FTIR is also practical for evaluating bacterial wood degradation [N2-R1].

So, for waterlogged wood:
- **Raman is especially good for lignin and aromatic structural features** [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is especially good for cellulose, hemicellulose, and functional-group-based analysis** [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- Both are useful for extractives and other non-structural components, though the evidence is more explicit for FTIR in this regard [N2-R3].

---

### 2) Main practical advantages

#### Raman advantages
- **Non-destructive sampling** is a major advantage. Raman is described as non-invasive and as offering advantages such as high speed, robust identification, low cost, and portability [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This is especially valuable for fragile waterlogged wood, where destructive sampling is undesirable [N1-R3].
- **Portable and in situ use** is also a practical strength. Portable Raman can enable in situ analysis without moving fragile remains [N1-R3].
- **Specific compound detection** is another strength. Raman can identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin in archaeological specimens [N1-R4], which can help distinguish extractive-like compounds and other organic markers [N1-R4].

#### FTIR advantages
- **Common laboratory availability** is a strong practical advantage. FTIR is described as practical in evaluating bacterial degradation in softwood and as widely used because it provides functional-group information [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Speed and routine use** are also important. The review notes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which future deterioration can be tracked, and that FTIR is among the most commonly reported methods for waterlogged archaeological wood [N6-F1]. This makes it a strong option for routine assessment or when sample numbers are large.
- **Functional-group resolution** is another benefit. FTIR is useful for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood because of its ability to provide information about functional groups [N2-R4].

So, if the priority is **portability, non-destructiveness, and specific compound detection**, Raman is often the better choice. If the priority is **common availability, speed, and routine functional-group analysis**, FTIR is often the better choice.

---

### 3) Main limitations

#### Raman limitations
- **Moisture and water content can affect signal quality and interpretation**. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood can have very high moisture content, and that moisture content is positively associated with deterioration [N3-F4]. While the evidence does not give a detailed Raman-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that moisture and deterioration alter the physical and chemical state of wood, which can affect how the sample is analyzed [N3-F4][N6-F1]. The review also states that Raman has been used in waterlogged archaeological wood conservation studies [N6-F1], indicating that researchers have already addressed moisture-related challenges, but the evidence does not specify what those exact solutions are [N6-F1].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are a major limitation. Waterlogged wood analysis often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling to avoid damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that the wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis, which implies some handling effort [N4-R4]. For Raman, this means the sample must be prepared carefully without excessive drying or mechanical stress, which can distort the structure and reduce the reliability of the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### FTIR limitations
- **Moisture and matrix background effects** are a major limitation. The evidence states that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where moisture can broaden peaks, create baseline shifts, or make interpretation more ambiguous [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are also important. Waterlogged wood often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis [N4-R4]. For FTIR, the main issue is that the sample must be prepared carefully, especially in the case of waterlogged wood, where drying or mounting can alter the structure and affect the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Interpretation complexity** is another limitation. The review notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous, with deterioration often occurring first at the surface and progressing inward, and that different species of erosion microorganisms produce different decay patterns [N6-F1]. This heterogeneity makes interpretation difficult, because the same spectrum may reflect different decay states or different regions of the same sample [N6-F1].

So, both methods have a major limitation in moisture-related signal complexity, but FTIR is more directly affected by moisture and matrix background effects [N5-F3], while Raman is more affected by preparation quality and handling of fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4].

---

### 4) How they differ in distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives

The evidence suggests that neither technique is universally superior for distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives, but they do differ in how well they can do so.

- **Raman is more reliable for lignin**. The evidence indicates that Raman can detect aromatic ring skeletal vibrations and is less susceptible to moisture interference [N5-F3]. It also says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods with differences and complementarity in feature-variable distributions [N5-R2].
- **FTIR is better for functional-group resolution**. The evidence says FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4], and that it can be used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood [N2-R4]. However, it also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This makes FTIR less reliable for unambiguous identification of individual components when the sample is highly heterogeneous or moist [N5-F3].
- **Both techniques face spectral overlap and ambiguity problems**. The evidence states that the feature-variable distributions differ between Raman and FTIR, but also that most peak positions in complex samples cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-R2][N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where the material is chemically and physically heterogeneous [N6-F1].

In short:
- If the goal is **specific lignin identification**, Raman may be more reliable [N5-F3].
- If the goal is **routine, functional-group-based analysis**, FTIR may be more reliable [N2-R4][N5-F3].
- If the goal is **unambiguous identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives**, both techniques face ambiguity, and neither is clearly superior in all cases [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

---

### 5) Which technique is better suited to waterlogged wood under different preservation conditions

The evidence points to a conditional conclusion:
- **Severely waterlogged or highly moist samples may favor Raman**. Because Raman is less susceptible to moisture interference, it may be better suited when the sample is very wet or when moisture is expected to complicate the signal [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Relatively stable or routinely handled samples may favor FTIR**. FTIR is widely used and accessible, making it a strong choice when the sample can be prepared and analyzed under controlled conditions [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Highly heterogeneous or degraded samples may require both techniques**. The review emphasizes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration patterns can vary by microorganism and burial environment [N6-F1]. In such cases, the best approach is often a multi-analytical strategy, because no single technique gives the best assessment [N6-F1].

So, the best choice depends on:
- **Moisture level**: Raman may be better for highly waterlogged wood [N5-F3].
- **Sample heterogeneity**: both techniques face ambiguity, but a combined approach is often better [N6-F1].
- **Practical constraints**: FTIR is more commonly available and faster, while Raman is more portable and non-destructive [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R4].

---

### 6) How complementary use of Raman and FTIR can improve interpretation

The evidence explicitly supports complementary use. The evidence says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods and that their feature-variable distributions differ [N5-R2]. It also says that spectral monitoring can reduce reliance on wet chemical analysis and improve detection of lignin removal [N5-F3]. In the context of waterlogged wood, this means:
- **Raman can provide more specific lignin and aromatic information**, especially in moist conditions [N5-F3].
- **FTIR can provide broader functional-group resolution and quantitative information**, especially when the sample is relatively stable [N2-R4].
- Together, they can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3].

The review also emphasizes that a multi-analytical approach is vital for obtaining a clear picture of the present state of decay [N6-F1]. This is important because waterlogged wood is chemically and physically heterogeneous, and because different preservation conditions may affect one technique more than the other [N6-F1].

---

### 7) Bottom-line conclusion

For **waterlogged archaeological wood**, the main conclusion is:

- **Raman is better when**: the sample is fragile, moisture-sensitive, or the goal is non-destructive, portable, or specific compound detection, especially for lignin [N1-R1][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is better when**: the sample can be prepared and analyzed under routine conditions, and the goal is accessible, fast, functional-group-based, or routine preservation assessment [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Neither is clearly superior for all preservation conditions**. Both face limitations from moisture, heterogeneity, and matrix effects [N3-F4][N5-F3][N6-F1].
- **Complementary use is often the best practical choice**. Combining Raman and FTIR can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

In short: Raman is the more modern, non-destructive, and moisture-tolerant option for some contexts; FTIR is the more established, accessible, and functional-group-oriented option for others. For waterlogged archaeological wood, the best approach is often to use both where possible, because no single technique alone gives the complete picture [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

## Main advantages and limitations of Raman versus FTIR for analyzing waterlogged archaeological wood

This comparison should be read as a practical guide to choosing between two complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods for waterlogged archaeological wood. The evidence from the branch reports shows that neither technique is universally superior for every preservation condition, but they do differ in how well they identify molecular components, handle moisture, and support interpretation. Below is a structured comparison of their main advantages and limitations.

---

### 1) What each method is best suited to identify

**Raman spectroscopy** is especially strong for identifying the major organic components in waterlogged wood, especially **lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose**. The evidence states that Raman spectra “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], and that Raman has been used in archaeological wood analysis to identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin [N1-R4]. It is also useful for detecting aromatic ring vibrations, which is important for lignin [N5-F3].

**FTIR** is also well suited to identifying the main molecular components of waterlogged wood, particularly **cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractives**. The evidence says FTIR and pyrolysis have been used to characterize wood components including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, extracts, and ash [N2-R3], and that FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4]. FTIR is also practical for evaluating bacterial wood degradation [N2-R1].

So, for waterlogged wood:
- **Raman is especially good for lignin and aromatic structural features** [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is especially good for cellulose, hemicellulose, and functional-group-based analysis** [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- Both are useful for extractives and other non-structural components, though the evidence is more explicit for FTIR in this regard [N2-R3].

---

### 2) Main practical advantages

#### Raman advantages
- **Non-destructive sampling** is a major advantage. Raman is described as non-invasive and as offering advantages such as high speed, robust identification, low cost, and portability [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This is especially valuable for fragile waterlogged wood, where destructive sampling is undesirable [N1-R3].
- **Portable and in situ use** is also a practical strength. Portable Raman can enable in situ analysis without moving fragile remains [N1-R3].
- **Specific compound detection** is another strength. Raman can identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin in archaeological specimens [N1-R4], which can help distinguish extractive-like compounds and other organic markers [N1-R4].

#### FTIR advantages
- **Common laboratory availability** is a strong practical advantage. FTIR is described as practical in evaluating bacterial degradation in softwood and as widely used because it provides functional-group information [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Speed and routine use** are also important. The review notes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which future deterioration can be tracked, and that FTIR is among the most commonly reported methods for waterlogged archaeological wood [N6-F1]. This makes it a strong option for routine assessment or when sample numbers are large.
- **Functional-group resolution** is another benefit. FTIR is useful for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood because of its ability to provide information about functional groups [N2-R4].

So, if the priority is **portability, non-destructiveness, and specific compound detection**, Raman is often the better choice. If the priority is **common availability, speed, and routine functional-group analysis**, FTIR is often the better choice.

---

### 3) Main limitations

#### Raman limitations
- **Moisture and water content can affect signal quality and interpretation**. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood can have very high moisture content, and that moisture content is positively associated with deterioration [N3-F4]. While the evidence does not give a detailed Raman-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that moisture and deterioration alter the physical and chemical state of wood, which can affect how the sample is analyzed [N3-F4][N6-F1]. The review also states that Raman has been used in waterlogged archaeological wood conservation studies [N6-F1], indicating that researchers have already addressed moisture-related challenges, but the evidence does not specify what those exact solutions are [N6-F1].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are a major limitation. Waterlogged wood analysis often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling to avoid damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that the wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis, which implies some handling effort [N4-R4]. For Raman, this means the sample must be prepared carefully without excessive drying or mechanical stress, which can distort the structure and reduce the reliability of the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### FTIR limitations
- **Moisture and matrix background effects** are a major limitation. The evidence states that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where moisture can broaden peaks, create baseline shifts, or make interpretation more ambiguous [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are also important. Waterlogged wood often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis [N4-R4]. For FTIR, the main issue is that the sample must be prepared carefully, especially in the case of waterlogged wood, where drying or mounting can alter the structure and affect the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Interpretation complexity** is another limitation. The review notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous, with deterioration often occurring first at the surface and progressing inward, and that different species of erosion microorganisms produce different decay patterns [N6-F1]. This heterogeneity makes interpretation difficult, because the same spectrum may reflect different decay states or different regions of the same sample [N6-F1].

So, both methods have a major limitation in moisture-related signal complexity, but FTIR is more directly affected by moisture and matrix background effects [N5-F3], while Raman is more affected by preparation quality and handling of fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4].

---

### 4) How they differ in distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives

The evidence suggests that neither technique is universally superior for distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives, but they do differ in how well they can do so.

- **Raman is more reliable for lignin**. The evidence indicates that Raman can detect aromatic ring skeletal vibrations and is less susceptible to moisture interference [N5-F3]. It also says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods with differences and complementarity in feature-variable distributions [N5-R2].
- **FTIR is better for functional-group resolution**. The evidence says FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4], and that it can be used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood [N2-R4]. However, it also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This makes FTIR less reliable for unambiguous identification of individual components when the sample is highly heterogeneous or moist [N5-F3].
- **Both techniques face spectral overlap and ambiguity problems**. The evidence states that the feature-variable distributions differ between Raman and FTIR, but also that most peak positions in complex samples cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-R2][N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where the material is chemically and physically heterogeneous [N6-F1].

In short:
- If the goal is **specific lignin identification**, Raman may be more reliable [N5-F3].
- If the goal is **routine, functional-group-based analysis**, FTIR may be more reliable [N2-R4][N5-F3].
- If the goal is **unambiguous identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives**, both techniques face ambiguity, and neither is clearly superior in all cases [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

---

### 5) Which technique is better suited to waterlogged wood under different preservation conditions

The evidence points to a conditional conclusion:
- **Severely waterlogged or highly moist samples may favor Raman**. Because Raman is less susceptible to moisture interference, it may be better suited when the sample is very wet or when moisture is expected to complicate the signal [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Relatively stable or routinely handled samples may favor FTIR**. FTIR is widely used and accessible, making it a strong choice when the sample can be prepared and analyzed under controlled conditions [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Highly heterogeneous or degraded samples may require both techniques**. The review emphasizes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration patterns can vary by microorganism and burial environment [N6-F1]. In such cases, the best approach is often a multi-analytical strategy, because no single technique gives the best assessment [N6-F1].

So, the best choice depends on:
- **Moisture level**: Raman may be better for highly waterlogged wood [N5-F3].
- **Sample heterogeneity**: both techniques face ambiguity, but a combined approach is often better [N6-F1].
- **Practical constraints**: FTIR is more commonly available and faster, while Raman is more portable and non-destructive [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R4].

---

### 6) How complementary use of Raman and FTIR can improve interpretation

The evidence explicitly supports complementary use. The evidence says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods and that their feature-variable distributions differ [N5-R2]. It also says that spectral monitoring can reduce reliance on wet chemical analysis and improve detection of lignin removal [N5-F3]. In the context of waterlogged wood, this means:
- **Raman can provide more specific lignin and aromatic information**, especially in moist conditions [N5-F3].
- **FTIR can provide broader functional-group resolution and quantitative information**, especially when the sample is relatively stable [N2-R4].
- Together, they can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3].

The review also emphasizes that a multi-analytical approach is vital for obtaining a clear picture of the present state of decay [N6-F1]. This is important because waterlogged wood is chemically and physically heterogeneous, and because different preservation conditions may affect one technique more than the other [N6-F1].

---

### 7) Bottom-line conclusion

For **waterlogged archaeological wood**, the main conclusion is:

- **Raman is better when**: the sample is fragile, moisture-sensitive, or the goal is non-destructive, portable, or specific compound detection, especially for lignin [N1-R1][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is better when**: the sample can be prepared and analyzed under routine conditions, and the goal is accessible, fast, functional-group-based, or routine preservation assessment [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Neither is clearly superior for all preservation conditions**. Both face limitations from moisture, heterogeneity, and matrix effects [N3-F4][N5-F3][N6-F1].
- **Complementary use is often the best practical choice**. Combining Raman and FTIR can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

In short: Raman is the more modern, non-destructive, and moisture-tolerant option for some contexts; FTIR is the more established, accessible, and functional-group-oriented option for others. For waterlogged archaeological wood, the best approach is often to use both where possible, because no single technique alone gives the complete picture [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

### 1) What each method is best suited to identify

**Raman spectroscopy** is especially strong for identifying the major organic components in waterlogged wood, especially **lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose**. The evidence states that Raman spectra “particularly reflect vibrational features of lignin, cellulose, and hemicelluloses” [N5-R1], and that Raman has been used in archaeological wood analysis to identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin [N1-R4]. It is also useful for detecting aromatic ring vibrations, which is important for lignin [N5-F3].

**FTIR** is also well suited to identifying the main molecular components of waterlogged wood, particularly **cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractives**. The evidence says FTIR and pyrolysis have been used to characterize wood components including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, extracts, and ash [N2-R3], and that FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4]. FTIR is also practical for evaluating bacterial wood degradation [N2-R1].

So, for waterlogged wood:
- **Raman is especially good for lignin and aromatic structural features** [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is especially good for cellulose, hemicellulose, and functional-group-based analysis** [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- Both are useful for extractives and other non-structural components, though the evidence is more explicit for FTIR in this regard [N2-R3].

---

### 2) Main practical advantages

#### Raman advantages
- **Non-destructive sampling** is a major advantage. Raman is described as non-invasive and as offering advantages such as high speed, robust identification, low cost, and portability [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This is especially valuable for fragile waterlogged wood, where destructive sampling is undesirable [N1-R3].
- **Portable and in situ use** is also a practical strength. Portable Raman can enable in situ analysis without moving fragile remains [N1-R3].
- **Specific compound detection** is another strength. Raman can identify organic compounds such as anthraquinone and copal resin in archaeological specimens [N1-R4], which can help distinguish extractive-like compounds and other organic markers [N1-R4].

#### FTIR advantages
- **Common laboratory availability** is a strong practical advantage. FTIR is described as practical in evaluating bacterial degradation in softwood and as widely used because it provides functional-group information [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Speed and routine use** are also important. The review notes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which future deterioration can be tracked, and that FTIR is among the most commonly reported methods for waterlogged archaeological wood [N6-F1]. This makes it a strong option for routine assessment or when sample numbers are large.
- **Functional-group resolution** is another benefit. FTIR is useful for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood because of its ability to provide information about functional groups [N2-R4].

So, if the priority is **portability, non-destructiveness, and specific compound detection**, Raman is often the better choice. If the priority is **common availability, speed, and routine functional-group analysis**, FTIR is often the better choice.

---

### 3) Main limitations

#### Raman limitations
- **Moisture and water content can affect signal quality and interpretation**. The evidence shows that waterlogged wood can have very high moisture content, and that moisture content is positively associated with deterioration [N3-F4]. While the evidence does not give a detailed Raman-specific moisture artifact mechanism, it does establish that moisture and deterioration alter the physical and chemical state of wood, which can affect how the sample is analyzed [N3-F4][N6-F1]. The review also states that Raman has been used in waterlogged archaeological wood conservation studies [N6-F1], indicating that researchers have already addressed moisture-related challenges, but the evidence does not specify what those exact solutions are [N6-F1].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are a major limitation. Waterlogged wood analysis often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling to avoid damaging fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that the wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis, which implies some handling effort [N4-R4]. For Raman, this means the sample must be prepared carefully without excessive drying or mechanical stress, which can distort the structure and reduce the reliability of the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### FTIR limitations
- **Moisture and matrix background effects** are a major limitation. The evidence states that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where moisture can broaden peaks, create baseline shifts, or make interpretation more ambiguous [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Sample preparation and handling issues** are also important. Waterlogged wood often requires drying, mounting, and careful handling [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that wood samples were mounted in a sample holder and rotated during analysis [N4-R4]. For FTIR, the main issue is that the sample must be prepared carefully, especially in the case of waterlogged wood, where drying or mounting can alter the structure and affect the signal [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Interpretation complexity** is another limitation. The review notes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous, with deterioration often occurring first at the surface and progressing inward, and that different species of erosion microorganisms produce different decay patterns [N6-F1]. This heterogeneity makes interpretation difficult, because the same spectrum may reflect different decay states or different regions of the same sample [N6-F1].

So, both methods have a major limitation in moisture-related signal complexity, but FTIR is more directly affected by moisture and matrix background effects [N5-F3], while Raman is more affected by preparation quality and handling of fragile samples [N4-R1][N4-R4].

---

### 4) How they differ in distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives

The evidence suggests that neither technique is universally superior for distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives, but they do differ in how well they can do so.

- **Raman is more reliable for lignin**. The evidence indicates that Raman can detect aromatic ring skeletal vibrations and is less susceptible to moisture interference [N5-F3]. It also says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods with differences and complementarity in feature-variable distributions [N5-R2].
- **FTIR is better for functional-group resolution**. The evidence says FTIR is widely used because it provides information about functional groups [N2-R4], and that it can be used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of wood [N2-R4]. However, it also notes that FTIR is affected by moisture and other matrix backgrounds in complex biomass samples, where most peak positions cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-F3]. This makes FTIR less reliable for unambiguous identification of individual components when the sample is highly heterogeneous or moist [N5-F3].
- **Both techniques face spectral overlap and ambiguity problems**. The evidence states that the feature-variable distributions differ between Raman and FTIR, but also that most peak positions in complex samples cannot be directly assigned to a single component [N5-R2][N5-F3]. This is especially important in waterlogged wood, where the material is chemically and physically heterogeneous [N6-F1].

In short:
- If the goal is **specific lignin identification**, Raman may be more reliable [N5-F3].
- If the goal is **routine, functional-group-based analysis**, FTIR may be more reliable [N2-R4][N5-F3].
- If the goal is **unambiguous identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives**, both techniques face ambiguity, and neither is clearly superior in all cases [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

---

### 5) Which technique is better suited to waterlogged wood under different preservation conditions

The evidence points to a conditional conclusion:
- **Severely waterlogged or highly moist samples may favor Raman**. Because Raman is less susceptible to moisture interference, it may be better suited when the sample is very wet or when moisture is expected to complicate the signal [N5-F3][N3-F4].
- **Relatively stable or routinely handled samples may favor FTIR**. FTIR is widely used and accessible, making it a strong choice when the sample can be prepared and analyzed under controlled conditions [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Highly heterogeneous or degraded samples may require both techniques**. The review emphasizes that waterlogged archaeological wood is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration patterns can vary by microorganism and burial environment [N6-F1]. In such cases, the best approach is often a multi-analytical strategy, because no single technique gives the best assessment [N6-F1].

So, the best choice depends on:
- **Moisture level**: Raman may be better for highly waterlogged wood [N5-F3].
- **Sample heterogeneity**: both techniques face ambiguity, but a combined approach is often better [N6-F1].
- **Practical constraints**: FTIR is more commonly available and faster, while Raman is more portable and non-destructive [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R4].

---

### 6) How complementary use of Raman and FTIR can improve interpretation

The evidence explicitly supports complementary use. The evidence says that Raman and FTIR are complementary vibrational spectroscopic methods and that their feature-variable distributions differ [N5-R2]. It also says that spectral monitoring can reduce reliance on wet chemical analysis and improve detection of lignin removal [N5-F3]. In the context of waterlogged wood, this means:
- **Raman can provide more specific lignin and aromatic information**, especially in moist conditions [N5-F3].
- **FTIR can provide broader functional-group resolution and quantitative information**, especially when the sample is relatively stable [N2-R4].
- Together, they can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of identification of cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3].

The review also emphasizes that a multi-analytical approach is vital for obtaining a clear picture of the present state of decay [N6-F1]. This is important because waterlogged wood is chemically and physically heterogeneous, and because different preservation conditions may affect one technique more than the other [N6-F1].

---

### 7) Bottom-line conclusion

For **waterlogged archaeological wood**, the main conclusion is:

- **Raman is better when**: the sample is fragile, moisture-sensitive, or the goal is non-destructive, portable, or specific compound detection, especially for lignin [N1-R1][N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **FTIR is better when**: the sample can be prepared and analyzed under routine conditions, and the goal is accessible, fast, functional-group-based, or routine preservation assessment [N2-R4][N6-F1].
- **Neither is clearly superior for all preservation conditions**. Both face limitations from moisture, heterogeneity, and matrix effects [N3-F4][N5-F3][N6-F1].
- **Complementary use is often the best practical choice**. Combining Raman and FTIR can reduce ambiguity and improve the reliability of distinguishing cellulose, lignin, and extractives [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].

In short: Raman is the more modern, non-destructive, and moisture-tolerant option for some contexts; FTIR is the more established, accessible, and functional-group-oriented option for others. For waterlogged archaeological wood, the best approach is often to use both where possible, because no single technique alone gives the complete picture [N5-R2][N5-F3][N6-F1].
